title: The Kids' Plate Tax
editorialNotes: The "$4 per plate" and "5 times a week" figures in the hook are anecdotal, not sourced; kept as headline-level scene copy.

thread.element: dinner plate emptying from overflowing to correctly portioned
thread.startState: overflowing plate, food spilling past the rim
thread.endState: small clean plate plus a full serving bowl beside it

copy.headline: Your kid ate three bites and left the rest.
You already know they won't finish it.
copy.body: You serve the full plate anyway. Here's why that's not a mistake - it's a reflex.

copy.headline: Children under 12 waste food served to them.
copy.body: For a family with two kids, that's plate waste alone - separate from the fridge waste figure.

copy.headline: It's not their fault.
items: Children's appetites are genuinely unpredictable - smaller humans with smaller stomachs who change their minds constantly.
The problem isn't the child. It's the portion.

copy.headline: The guilt loop:
items: scrape the rest into the trash
serve a full plate again next time
copy.body: The loop never breaks because emotion overrides the math.

copy.headline: The fix isn't portion-control lectures. It's "start small, seconds free."
items: Serve half. If they want more, they ask.
Restaurants call this coursing. Parents can call it not throwing $4 away.

copy.headline: The 3-step reset:
items: 2) Let them ask for seconds - don't offer first.
3) Praise the ask, not the clean plate.

copy.headline: You're not wasting food because you're a bad parent. You're wasting food because you were taught a full plate means love.
copy.ctaLine: fond helps you track what your household actually eats - so you serve what gets used.
